newsitem.title: USA: Only one glove at murder scene, Simpson jury told.
newsitem.headline: Only one glove at murder scene, Simpson jury told.

text.p: The first police officers to arrive at Nicole Brown Simpson's home after she and Ronald Goldman were murdered testified Monday that they saw only a single bloody glove at the crime scene.
Officer Robert Riske testified to finding a blue knit cap and the single leather glove under a plant near Goldman's body about two hours before Detective Mark Fuhrman arrived.
His partner, Officer Miguel Terrazas, said that during the five hours he was at the scene in the early hours of June 13, 1994, he saw only one bloody glove.
And their supervisor, Sgt. David Rossi, told jurors that he saw only one glove and that nobody -- including then-detective Fuhrman -- moved it or any other evidence that night.
Simpson was acquitted last October of criminal charges in connection with the June 12, 1994, murders.

The former football star, Hollywood actor and television pitchman is battling a wrongful-death civil lawsuit filed by the victims' families, who are seeking financial damages for the loss of their loved ones.

Fuhrman, who earlier this month pleaded no contest to a single charge of perjury over his past use of racial slurs, was painted by the defence in the criminal case as a racist rogue cop who planted evidence against Simpson. Lawyers in the civil case have said they will use similar tactics.
The officers' testimony could help the plaintiffs discount a defence contention that Fuhrman took a glove from the scene and planted it on Simpson's property.
Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki Monday dealt the defence a setback when he effectively ruled that Simpson's lawyers could not introduce much of their theory about bungled evidence collection by the police.
"This is not a case against the Los Angeles Police Department for committing malpractice. The defendant is not suing the LAPD," he said.
"Whether or not the police department did or did not act within certain protocols of investigation ... is immaterial," he added.
The judge told lawyers for Simpson that those items the department failed to collect were irrelevant because they were no longer evidence.

Among those items the judge barred the defence from introducing were: a scrap of paper seen in photographs near the bodies but never collected, a spot of blood from Nicole Brown Simpson's back which was ordered to be collected but never was and a lens from her mother's glasses which disappeared from the LAPD crime lab.

Riske, the first police officer to testify in the civil trial, described how he and Terrazas arrived at Nicole Brown Simpson's condominium, where they were flagged down by neighbours and directed to the bodies.
"I looked down the walkway and saw a female white with a black dress and blonde hair," Riske said. "There was blood approximately half-way down the walkway," he added.
He said he called additional units to the scene, then moved closer and "saw the body of Mr. Goldman lying against the north fence."
Shown a grim photo of Goldman's blood-soaked body lying in the dirt, the officer used a wooden pointer to show jurors the evidence he discovered that night.
"There's a glove and a hat underneath the plant," he said.

Ronald Goldman's father, Fred, wept as the photograph of his bloodied son was shown on a large television screen. Jurors studied the photos of the crime scene and victims intently, several apparently taking notes.

Terrazas, cross-examined by Simpson's lead attorney, Robert Baker, also agreed the crime scene was "awash with blood" and said there was "a river of blood" coming from the stabbed and slashed body of Nicole Brown Simpson and flowing down the walkway of her condominium.
Riske said there were 14 police officers in and around Nicole Brown Simpson's condo before Fuhrman and his partner, Ron Phillips, arrived at the scene.
